speeches.Maior: My Lords, as you are liege men to the Crowne, True noblemen, and subiects to the King, Attend his Highnesse proclamation, Commaunded by the Iudges of Assise, For keeping peace at this assemblie. What haue you searcht the towne? Surely my lord of Rochester was then deceiude, Or ill informde of sir Iohn Old-castle, Or if he came this way, hees past the towne, He could not else haue scapt you in the search. What thinke you best to do? Come I pray you, and be circumspect. exeunt Vat mester, you counterfeit rebell, this shall no • serue your turne. You counterfeit, this shal not serue you, weele tor ture you, weele make you to confesse where that arch-here tique Lord Cobham is: come binde him fast. And perceiuing the house beset, would get away: stand sirra. Sirra, weele finde you an Irish man before we part: lay hold vpon him. Oh tis Lankashire carier, let him passe. VVe are come to seeke for some suspected persons, and such as heere we found, haue apprehended. Mine hoste, know you this man? That was that villaine traitour Old-castle, that thus escaped vs: make out • uy and cry yet after him, keepe fast that traiterous rebell his seruant there: farewell mine hoste. The Lord Powes if it like your honor, And this his Lady, trauelling toward Wales, Who for they lodgde last night within my house, And my Lord Bishop did lay search for such, Were very willing to come on with me, Lest for their sakes, suspition we might wrong.
Serieant, without the ceremonie of O yes. Pronoune alowd the proclamation.
The Kings Iustices, perceiuing what publique mis chiefe may ensue this priuate quarrel in his maiesties name do straightly charge and commaund all persons, of what degree soeuer, to depart this cittie of Hereford, except such as are bound to giue attendance at this Assise, and that no man pre sume to weare any weapon, especially welsh-hookes, forrest billes. And that the Lord Powesse do presently disperse and discharge his retinue, and depart the cittie in the Kings peace, he and his followers, on paine of imprisonment. No, hee's gone farre enough.
Peace, and heare the proclamation. Officers assist.
Where's the Lord Herbert? is he hurt or slaine?
How fares hid Lordshippe, friends? Yet let search be made, To apprehend his followers that are left.
speeches.1. Iud: Conuay him hence, let not his wounds take ayre, And get him dress'd with expedition, Ex. Herb. & Gough M. Maior of Hereford M Snriue o'th shire, Commit Lord Powesse to safe custodie, To answer the disturbance of the peace, Lord Herberts perill, and his high contempt Of vs, and you the Kings commissioners, See it be done with care and diligence.
speeches.1. Iudge: Away with them. To Iayle with them, and the Lord Herberts men, Weele talke with them, when the Assise is done, Exeunt. Riotous, audacious, and vnruly Groomes, Must we be forced to come from the Bench, To quiet brawles, which euery Constable In other ciuill places can suppresse? This case concernes the Kings prerogatiue, And • s dangerous to the State and common wealth. Gentlemen, Iustices, master Maior, and master Shrieue, It doth behoue vs all, and each of vs In generall and particular, to haue care For the suppressing of all mutinies, And all assemblies, except souldiers musters For the Kings preparation into France. We heare of secret conuenticles made, And there is doubt of some conspiracies, Which may breake out into rebellious armes When the King's gone, perchance before he go: Note as an instance, this one perillous fray, What factions might haue growne on either part, To the destruction of the King and Realme, Yet, in my conscience, sir Iohn Old-castle Innocent of it, onely his name was vsde. We therefore from his Highnesse giue this charge. You maister Maior, looke to your citizens, You maister Sherife vnto your shire, and you As Iustices in euery ones precinct There be no meetings. When the vulgar sort Sit on their Ale-bench, with their cups and kannes, Matters of state be not their common talke, Nor pure religion by their lips prophande. Let vs returne vnto the Bench againe, And there examine further of this fray. Enter a Baily and a Serieant
speeches.2. Iudge: What Bale? what suerties? What was the quarrel that causde all this stirre?
Two of the most, sufficient are ynow,
They that are left behind, shall answer all. Exeunt.
speeches.Suffolke: Now my lord Bishop, take free liberty To speake your minde: what is your sute to vs? What proofe is there against them to be had, That what you say the law may iustifie? With pardon of your Highnesse (my dread lord) Such little sparkes neglected, may in time Grow to a mighty flame: but thats not all, He doth beside maintaine a strange religion, And will not be compelld to come to masse. Not where Religion is the plea, my lord.
speeches.Bishop: My noble Lord, no more than what you know, And haue bin oftentimes inuested with: Grieuous complaints haue past betweene the lippes Of enuious persons to vpbraide the Cleargy, Some carping at the liuings which we haue, And others spurning at the ceremonies That are of auncient custome in the church. Amongst the which, Lord Cobham is a chiefe: What inconuenience may proceede hereof, Both to the King and to the common wealth, May easily be discernd, when like a frensie This innouation shall possesse their mindes. These vpstarts will haue followers to vphold Their damnd opinion, more than Harry shall To vndergoe his quarrell gainst the French. They giue themselues the name of Protestants, And meete in fields and solitary groues. To summon him vnto the Arches, Where such offences haue their punishment. It is, my lord. He cannot (my Lord) in such a case as this. Yea, yea, sir Iohn, if he would keepe his word, But I perceiue he fauours him so much, As this will be to small effect, I feare. And well remembred, I will haue it so, A Sumner shall be sent about it strait Exit. Iustice dread Soueraigne. As thou art King, so graunt I may haue iustice. I tell ye Lady, its not possible But you should know where he conueies himselfe, And you haue hid him in some secret place. Go to, go to ye are an heretike, And will be forc'de by torture to confesse, If faire meanes will not serue to make ye tell. Your husband is a dangerous schismaticke, Traitor to God, the King, and common wealth, And therefore master Croamer shrieue of Kent, I charge you take her to your custodie, And ceaze the goods of Sir John Old-castle To the Kings vse, let her go in no more, To fetch so much as her apparell out, There is your warrant from his maiestie. No, turne her out of doores, L. Warden and Oldcastle whisper. Euen as she is, and leade him to the Tower, With guard enough for feare of rescuing. What intricate confusion haue we heere? Not two houres since we apprehended one, In habite Irish, but in speech, not so: And now you bring another, that in speech Is altogether Irish, but in habite Seemes to be English: yea and more than so, The seruant of that heretike Lord Cobham. Otherwise calld Harpoole of Kent, go to sit, You cannot blinde vs with your broken Irish. Well, our affaires doe call vs backe to London, So that we cannot prosecute the cause As we desire to do, therefore we leaue The charge with you, to see they be conuaide To Hartford Sise: both this counterfaite And you sir Iohn of Wrotham, and your wench, For you are culpable as well as they, Though not for murder, yet for felony. But since you are the meanes to bring to light This gracelesse murder, you shall beare with you, Our letters to the Iudges of the bench, To be your friendes in what they lawfull may.
speeches.sir Ihon: Was euer heard (my Lord) the like til now? That theeues and rebells, s bloud heretikes, Playne heretikes, Ile stand toote to their teeth, Should haue to colour, their vile practises, A title of such worth, as Protestant? enter one wyth a letter. Pay all: this is some lucke. What if they do?
O but you must not sweare, it ill becomes One of your coate, to rappe out bloudy oathes. A fire that must be quencht; wel, say no more, The King anon goes to the counsell chamber, There to debate of matters touching France: As he doth passe by, Ile informe his grace Concerning your petition: Master Butler, If I forget, do you remember me, I thanke them, my Lord Bishop, for their loue, But will not take their mony, if you please To giue it to this gentleman, you may. It was my Lord, but very wrongfully. And still they vow my gracious Lord to be so, Hoping your maiestie will thinke of them, As of your louing subiects, and suppresse All such malitious errors as begin To spot their calling, and disturb the church. No new my Lord, the old is great enough, And so increasing as if not cut downe, Will breede a scandale to your royall state, And set your Kingdome quickely in an vproare, The Kentish knight Lord Cobham, in despight Of any law, or spirituall discipline, Maintaines this vpstart new religion still, And diuers great assemblies by his meanes And priuate quarrells, are commenst abroad, As by this letter more at large my liege, Is made apparant. Send poast my Lord to fetch him backe againe. I go my Soueraigne with all happie speede. exit
Pardon him good my Lord, it is his zeale, An honest country prelate, who laments To see such foule disorder in the church. That is our sute, my Lord, that he be tane, And brought in question for his heresie, Beside, two letters brought me out of Wales, Wherin my Lord Herford writes to me, What tumult and sedition was begun, About the Lord Cobham, at the Sises there, For they had much ado to calme the rage, And that the valiant Herbert is there slaine. Not for a recompence, But as a token of our loue to you, By me my Lords of the cleargie do present This purse, and in it full a thousand Angells, Praying your Lordship to accept their gift. Sir, then we craue your furtherance herein. Nay, pray ye take it, trust me but you shal, But in his name the quarrell did begin, About the opinion which he held (my hege.) We do beseech you therefore gracious prince, Without offence vnto your maiesty We may be bold to vse authoritie. Ah my good Lord, the state's abusde, And our decrees most shamefully prophande. Euen by this heretike, This Iew, this Traitor to your maiestie. Thus mightie King, by generall consent, A messenger was sent to cite this Lord, To make appearance in the consis • orie, And comming to his house, a ruffian slaue, One of his daily followers, met the man, Who knowing him to be a parator, Assaults him first, and after in contempt Of vs, and our proceedings, makes him eate The written processe, parchment, seale and all: Whereby his maister neither was brought forth, Nor we but scornd, for our authoritie. At sixe a clocke this morning. But it was done my lord by his appointment, Or else his man durst ne're haue bin so bold. I could haue told your maiestie as much Before he went, but that I saw your Grace Was too much blinded by his flaterie. This falls out well, and at the last I hope Exeunt To see this heretike die in a rope. Where is my Lord the King? health to your grace, Examining my Lord some of these caitiue rebels, It is a generall voyce amongst them all, That they had neuer come vnto this place, But to haue met their valiant general, The good Lord Cobham as they title him, Whereby, my Lord, your grace may now perceiue, His treason is apparant, which before He sought to colour by his flattery. It is but counterfeit, my gracious lords, And therefore may it please your maiestie, To set your hand vnto this precept here, By which weel cause him forthwith to appeare, And answer this by order of the law. It shall be done, my Lord, without delay: So now I hold Lord Cobham in my hand, That which shall finish thy disdained life. Then let her confesse Where Old-castle her husband is conceald. If my Lord Warden? nay then I charge you, That all the cinque Ports whereof you are chief • Be laid forthwith, that he escape vs not, Shew him his highnesse warrant M. Shrieue. Peace, he comes here, now do your office. Yea of high treason, traitor, heretike. VVhat thou art, the kings hand shall testifie, Shewt him Lord Warden. We are not bound to do kind office • For any traitor, schismatike, nor heretike, The kings hand is our warrant for our worke, Who is departed on his way for France, And at Southhampton doth repose this night. What, to Southhampton? Vrge it no more, for if an Angell spake, I sweare by sweet saint Peters blessed keyes, First goes he to the Tower, then to the stake. No hate of mine, but power of holy church, Fo • bids all fauor to false heretikes. This old iniquitie, this heretike? That in contempt of our church discipline, Compeld my Sumner to deuoure his processet Old Ruffian past-grace, vp start schismatike, Had not the King prayd vs to pardon ye, Ye had fryed for it, ye grizild heretike. VVel, God forgiue him and I pardon him. Let him attend his master in the Tower, For I in charity wish his soule no hurt. Tooth Tower with him, and when my leisure serues, I will examine him of Articles, Looke my lord Warden as you haue in charge, The Shriue performe his office. VVhat bringst thou there? what? bookes of heresie. Away with them, to'th fire with them Clun, Now fie vpon these vpstart heretikes, Al English, burne them, burne them quickly Clun. Now you haue brought me heere into the Tower, You may go backe vnto the Porters Lodge, And send for drinke or such things as you want, Where if I haue occasion to imploy you, Ile send some officer to cal you to me. Into the cittie go not, I commaund you, Perhaps I may haue present neede to vse you. Do so I pray you. Ho, M. Lieftenant. A friend of yours. Sir heres my warrant from the Counsell, For conference with sir Iohn Old-castle, Vpon some matter of great consequence. I did sir, and nothing repent it I assure you. M. Lieftenant I pray you giue vs leaue, I must conferre here with sir Iohn a little. Sir Iohn I am come vnto you from the lords of his highnesse most honorable counsell, to know if yet you do re cant your errors, conforming you vnto the holy church. What meanes? thou heretike? Darst thou but lift thy hand against my calling? Clubbes clubs, clubs. So, away with them. exeunt.
speeches.Sir Iohn: Theres one they call him Sir Iohn Old-castle, He has not his name for naught: for like a castle Doth he encompasse them within his walls, But till that castle be subuerted quite, We ne're shall be at quiet in the realme. Stand true-man saies a thiefe? Stand thiefe too.
I will my Lord. Offer him a purse. The best I can my Lord of Rochester. Heere, here. Enter Butler. Here sir here. Traitor vnto his country, how he smooth'de, And seemde as innocent as Truth it selfe? I goe my Soueraigne. My Lord. I will my Lord. exit Hold villaines hold, my Lords, what do ye meane, To see a traitor draw against the King? Please it your Highnesse, it is breake of day, And as I skouted neere to Islington, The gray ey'd morning gaue me glimmering, Of armed men comming downe Hygate hill, Who by their course are coasting hitherward. Didst thou not rob me?
speeches.sir I • hn: Were ye all three vpon New Market heath, You should not neede straine curtsie who should ha'te, Sir Iohn would quickely rid ye of that care. Alas twas ignoran • e and want, my gracious liege.
speeches.Suf: The King is comming, feare ye not my Lord, The very first thing I will breake with him, Shal be about your matter. Enter K. Harry and Hunting ton in talke.
My Lord of Suffolke, Was it not saide the Cleargy did refuse To lend vs mony toward our warres in France? I know it was, for Huntington here tells me, They haue bin very bountifull of late. God else forbid: why Suffolke, is there Any new rupture to disquiet them? We do find it here, There was in Wales a certaine fray of late, Betweene two noblemen, but what of this? Followes it straight Lord Cobham must be he Did cause the same? I dare be sworne (good knight) He neuer dreampt of any such contention. How if it did? was either he in place, To take part with them, or abette them in it? If brabling fellowes, whose in kindled bloud, Seethes in their fiery vaines, will needes go fight, Making their quarrells of some words that passt, Either of you, or you, amongst their cuppes, Is the fault yours, or are they guiltie of it? We would be loath to presse our subiects bodies, Much lesse their soules, the deere redeemed part, Of him that is the ruler of vs all, Yet let me counsell ye, that might command, Do not presume to tempt them with ill words, Nor suffer any meetings to be had Within your house, but to the vttermost, Disperse the flockes of this new gathering sect. Let it suffice we know your loyaltie, What haue you there? But yet it is not signed with our hand. The fact, you say, was done, Not of prepensed malice, but by chance. There is his pardon, bid him make amends, writes. And cleanse his soule to God for his offence, What we remit, is but the bodies scourge, Enter Bishop. How now Lord Bishop? What meanes this exclamation, let vs know? How, or by whom? Forbeare I say, and Bishop, shew the cause From whence this late abuse hath bin deriu'de, When was this done? And when came you to court? By this it seemes, he is not guilty of it, And you haue done him wrong t'accuse him so. Or else you durst be bold, to interrupt, And fill our eares with friuolous complaints, Is this the duetie you do beare to vs? Was't not sufficient we did passe our word To send for him, but you misdoubting it, Or which is worse, intending to forestall Our regall power, must likewise summon him? This sauours of Ambition, not of zeale, And rather proues, you malice his estate, Than any way that he offends the law. Go to, we like it not, and he your officer, That was imployde so much amisse herein, Had his desert for being insolent: Enter Huntington So Cobham when you please you may depart. Farewell, what's the newes by Huntington? So nere our presence? dare they be so bold? And will prowd warre, and eager thirst of bloud, Whom we had thought to entertaine farre off, Presse forth vpon vs in our natiue boundes? Must wee be forc't to hansell our sharp blades In England here, which we prepar'd for France? Well, a Gods name be it, what's their number? say, Or who's the chiefe commander of this rowt? How, the Lord Cobham? I cannot thinke it yet, he would be false, But if he be, no matter let him go, Weele meet both him and them vnto their wo. Trippe Dicke, Trippe George. they trippe. George, you are out. Giue me the dice, I passe for twentie pound, Heres to our luckie passage into France. Master Parson? we play nothing but gold? Set priest set, I passe for all that gold. Out sir, pay all. No crackt french crownes? I hope to see more crackt french crownes ere long. Giue me the dice, tis I must shread the priest: At all sir Iohn. Ile cast better yet. I passe for all. Set parson, set, the dice die in my hand: When parson, when? what can ye finde no more? Alreadie drie? wast you bragd of your store? Yea, and Ile couer it. Nay tarry priest, ye shall not leaue vs yet, Do not these peeces fit each other well? Thereby beginnes a tale: There was a thiefe, in face much like sir Iohn, But t'was not hee, that thiefe was all in greene, Met me last day on Blacke Heath, neere the parke, With him a woman, I was al alone, And weaponlesse, my boy had al my • oo •• s, And was before prouiding me a boate: Short tale to make, sir Iohn, the thiefe I meane, Tooke a iust hundreth pound in gold from me. I storm'd at it, and 〈◊〉 be reueng'de If ere we met, he like a 〈…〉 , Brake with his teeth this 〈◊〉 • ust in two, To be a token at our meeting next, Prouided, I should charge no Officer To apprehend him, but at weapons point Recouer that, and what he had beside. Well met sir Iohn, betake ye to your tooles By torch light, for master parson you are he That had my gold. A greede, I charge ye do not boudge a foot, Sir Iohn haue at ye. Butler what newes? why dost thou trouble vs? Let vs withdraw, my Lords, prepare our troopes, To charge the rebels, if there be such cause, For this lawd priest this diuellish hypocrite, That is a thiefe, a gamster, and what not, Let him be hang'd vp for example sake. Wil a true subiect robb • his King? Twas want of grace: why, you should be as salt To season others with good document, Your liues as lampes to giue the people light, As shepheards, not as wolues to spoile the flock, Go hang hm Butler. I confesse I haue, But I repent and haue reclaimd my selfe. Wilt thou? my lords, will you be his suerties? And we will grant thee that, Liue and repent, and proue an honest man, Which when I heare, and safe returne from France, Ile giue thee liuing, till when take thy gold, But spend it better then at cards or wine, For better vertues fit that coate of thine. Bring in those traitors, whose aspiring minds, Thought to haue triumpht in our ouerthrow, But now ye see, base villaines, what successe Attends ill actions wrongfully attempted. Sir Roger Acton, thou retainst the name Of knight, and shouldst be more discreetly temperd, Than ioyne with peasants, gentry is diuine, But thou hast made it more then popular. Thy conscience? then thy conscience is corrupt, For in thy conscience thou art bound to vs, And in thy conscience thou shouldst loue thy country, Else what s the difference twixt a Christian, And the vnciuil manners of the Turke? Reforme Religion? was it that ye sought? I pray who gaue you that authority? Belike then we do hold the scepter vp, And sit within the throne but for a cipher, Time was, good subiects would make knowne their griefe, And pray amendment, not inforce the same, Vnlesse their King were tyrant, which I hope You cannot iustly say that Harry is, What is that other? Sirra what made you leaue your barly broth, To come in armour thus against your King? And so you brought those horses which we saw, Trapt all in costly furniture, and meant To weare these spurs when you were knighted once. In and out vppon occasion, therefore you shall be hang'd, and in the sted of wearing these spurres vpon your heeles, about your necke they shall bewray your folly to the world. That comes too late: but tell me, went there none Beside sir Roger Acton, vpon whom You did depend to be your gouernour? Beares he part in this conspiracie. enter Bishop But did he promise you that he would come. Now by my ro • altie I would haue sworne, But for his conscience, which I beare withall, There had not liude a more true hearted subiect. Bishop, not only that, but take commission, To search, attach, imprison, and condemne, This most notorious traitor as you please. I thinke the yron age begins but now, (Which learned poets haue so often taught) Wherein there is no credit to be giuen, To either wordes, or lookes, or solemne oathes, For if there were, how often hath he sworne, How gently tun'de the musicke of his tongue, And with what amiable face beheld he me, When all, God knowes, was but hypocrisie. enter Cobham. Ah villaine, canst thou wish prosperitie, Whose heart includeth naught but treacherie? I do arrest thee here my selfe, false knight, Of treason capitall against the state. Thy necke shall feele it is in earnest shortly, Darst thou intrude into our presence, knowing How haynously thou hast offended vs? But this is thy accustomed deceit, Now thou perceiust thy purpose is in vaine, With some excuse or other thou wilt come, To cleere thy selfe of this rebellion. If you deny it, here is euidence, See you these men, you neuer councelled, Nor offerd them assistance in their warres No, didst not say that sir Iohn Old-castle, Was one with whom you purposde to haue met? Was there no other argument but that? The more pernitious you to taint him then, Whome you knew not was faulty yea or no. Earle Cambridge, Scroope, and Gray corrupted With bribes from Charles of France, either to winne My Crowne from me, or secretly contriue My death by treason? Is this possible? Oh neuer heard of base ingratitude! Euen those I hugge within my bosome most, Are readiest euermore to sting my heart. Pardon me Cobham, I haue done thee wrong, Heereafter I will liue to make amends. Is then their time of meeting so neere hand? Weele meete with them, but little for their ease, If God permit: goe take these rebells hence, Let them haue martiall law: but as for thee, Friend to thy king and country, still be free. Exeunt. That were a shame indeede, no, sit againe, And you shall haue my counsell in this case, If you can find no way to kill this King, Then you shall see how I can further ye, Scroopes way by poison was indifferent, But yet being bed-fellow vnto the King, And vnsuspected sleeping in his bosome, In mine opinion, that's the likelier way, For such f • lse friends are able to do much, And silent night is Treason's fittest friend, Now, Cambridge in his setting hence for France, Or by the way, or as he goes aboord, To do the deed, that was indifferent too, Yet somewhat doubtful; might I speake my mind, For many reasons needelesse now to vrge. Mary Lord Gray came something neare the point, To haue the King at councell, and there murder him, As Caesar was amongst his dearest friends: None like to that, if all were of his mind. Tell me oh tel me you • right honors staines, For which of all my kindnesses to you, Are ye become thus traitors to your king? And France must haue the spoile of Harries life? How pardon ye • that were a sinne indeed, Drag them to death, which iustly they deserue, they leade them away. And France shall dearely buy this villany, So soone as we set footing on her breast, God haue the praise for our deliuerance, And next, our thankes (Lord Cobham) is to thee, True perfect mirror of nobilitie. exeunt.
speeches.Harry: As how? To answere personally, is that your meaning? How if he appeale? I tooke it alwayes, that our selfe stoode out, As a sufficient refuge, vnto whome Not any but might lawfully appeale. But weele not argue now vpon that poynt: For sir Iohn Old-castle whom you accuse, Let me intreate you to dispence awhile With your high title of preheminence. in scorne. Report did neuer yet condemne him so, But he hath alwayes beene reputed loyall: And in my knowledge I can say thus much, That he is vertuous, wise, and honourable: If any way his conscience be seduc'de, To wauer in his faith: Ile send for him, And schoole him priuately, if that serue not, Then afterward you may proceede against him. Butler, be you the messenger for vs, And will him presently repaire to court. exeunt. Tis not enough Lord Cobham to submit. You must forsake your grosse opinion, The Bishops find themselues much iniured, And though for some good seruice you haue done, We for our part are pleasde to pardon you, Yet they will not so soone be satisfied, Priest, hast thou any more?
speeches.sir Iohn: How now my lord, why stand you discontent? In sooth, me thinkes the King hath well decreed. Why then Ile tell you what y'are best to do: If you suspect the King will be but cold In reprehending him, send you a processe too To serue vpon him: so you may be sure To make him answer't, howsoere it fall. Yea, doe so, in the meane space this remaines For kinde sir Iohn of Wrotham honest Iacke. Me thinkes the purse of gold the Bishop gaue, Made a good shew, it had a tempting looke, Beshrew me, but my fingers ends do itch To be vpon those rudduks: well, tis thus: I am not as the worlde does take me for: If euer woolfe were cloathed in sheepes coate, Then I am he, olde huddle and twang, yfaith, A priest in shew, but in plaine termes, a th • efe, Yet let me tell you too, an honest theefe. One that will take it where it may besp. And spend it freely in good fellowship. I haue as many shapes as Proteus had, That still when any villany is done, There may be none suspect it was sir Iohn. Besides, to comfort me, for whats this life, Except the crabbed bitternes thereof Be sweetened now and then with lechery? I haue my Doll, my concubine as t'were, To frollicke with, a lusty bounsing gerle. But whilst I loyter here the gold, may scape, And that must not be so, it is mine owne, Therefore Ile meete him on his way to court, And shriue him of it: there will be the sport. Exit. A good fellow. I must make you find some before we part, if you haue no mony you shal haue ware, as many sound drie blows as your skin can carrie. Sirra no more adoe, come, come, giue me the mony you haue, dispatch, I cannot stand all day. How much is there on't of thy word? From whence cam'st thou? Art thou one of the Kings seruants? I am glad thou art no worse, thou maist the better spare thy mony, & thinkst thou thou mightst get a poor thiefe his pardon if he should haue neede. Wilt thou do so much for me, when I shall haue oc casion? Nay, I am a pittifull thiefe, all the hurt I do a man, I take but his purse, Ile kill no man. Giue me thy hand of the same. Me thinks the King should be good to theeues be cause he has bin a thiefe himselfe, though I thinke now he be turned true-man. How? because he once robde me before I fell to the trade my selfe, when that foule villainous guts, that led him to all that rogery, was in's company there, that Fal staffe. Not I yfaith. Well, if old King Henry had liu'de, this King that is now, had made theeuing the best trade in England. Because he was the chiefe warden of our compa ny, it's pittie that ere he should haue bin a King, he was so braue a thiefe, but sirra, wilt remember my pardon if neede be? Wilt thou? well then because thou shalt go safe, for thou mayest hap (being so earely) be met with againe, be fore thou come to Southwarke, if any man when he should bid thee good morrow, bid thee stand, say thou but sir Iohn, and he will let thee passe. Nay sirra, because I thinke indeede I shall haue some occasion to vse thee, & as thou comst oft this way, I may light on thee another time not knowing thee, here, ile breake this Angell, take thou halfe of it, this is a token betwixt thee and me. O my fine golden slaues, heres for thee wench yfaith, now Dol, we wil reuel in our beuer, this is a tyth pigge of my vicaridge, God haue mercy neigbour Shooters hill, you paid your tyth honestly. Wel I heare there is a company of re belles vp against the King, got together in Ficket field neere Holborne, and as it is thought here in Kent, the King will be there to night in's owne person, well ile to the Kings camp, and it shall go hard, but if there be any doings, Ile make some good boote amongst them. exit. Edge ye good fellowes, take a fresh gamster in. Ye passe indeede. Zounds what a question's that? I tell thee I haue more then all you three, At these ten Angells. Yfaith but one, dost wonder how I come by gold? I wonder rather how poore souldiers should haue gold, for Ile tell thee good fellow, we haue euery day tythes, offerings, christnings, weddings, burialls: and you poore snakes come seldome to a bootie. Ile speake a prowd word, I haue but one parsonage, Wrootham, tis better than the Bishopprick of Ro chester, theres nere a hill, heath, nor downe in all Kent, but tis in my parish, Barrham downe, Chobham downe, Gads hill, Wrootham hill, Blacke heath, Cockes heath, Birchen wood, all pay me tythe, gold quoth a? ye passe not for that. Sbloud pay me angel gold, Ile none of your crackt French crownes nor pistolets, Pay me faire angel gold, as I pay you. Thou meanest of French mens crownes, when the King is in France. The diuell and all is yours: at that: sdeath, what • asting is this? Then Ile be hangd. Sirra, hast thou not giuen thy soule to the diuell for casting? Thou passest all that ere I playde withall: Sirra, dost thou not cogge, nor foist, nor slurre? Alls gone but that. Why sir, tis gold. The diuell do ye good on't, I am blinde, yee haue blowne me vp. Zounds I won't in play, in faire square play of the keeper of Eltham parke, and that I will maintaine with this poore whinyard, be you two honest men to stand and looke vpon's, and let's alone, and take neither part. Souldier ware your skonce. The King! Gods wil, I am in a proper pickle. Not so my gracious soueraigne, I confesse I am a frayle man, flesh and bloud as other are: but set my imperfecti ons aside, by this light ye haue not a taller man ▪ nor a truer sub iect to the Crowne and State, than sit 〈◊〉 of VVrootham. I must confesse I saw some of your gold, but my dread Lord, I am in no humor for death, therfore saue my life, God will that sinners liue; do not you cause me die, once in their liues the best may goe astray, and if the world say true, your selfe (my liege) haue bin a thiefe. So will I do if you will giue me time. Viuat Rex & currat lex, my liege, if ye haue cause of battell, ye shal see sir Iohn of Wrootham bestirre himselfe in your quarrel. exeunt. In and out vpon ocasion, that goes hard. No not to hurt yon for a thousand pound, Come Dol, come, be mery wench, Farewell Kent, we are not for thee, Be lusty my lasse, come for Lancashi • e, We must nip the Boung for these crownes. Gone Doll, gone, flowne, spent, vanished, the diuel, drinke and the dice, has deuoured all. No Dol, no, ile none of that, Kent • s too hot Doll, Kent's too hot: the weathercocke of Wrotham will crow no longer, we haue pluckt him, he has lost his feathers, I haue prunde him bare, left him thrice, is moulted, is moulted, we ̄ ch. Peace Doll, peace, come mad wench, Ile make thee an honest woman, weele into Lancashire to our friends, the troth is, Ile marry thee, we want but a little mony to buy vs a horse, and to spend by the way, the next sheep that comes shal loose his fleece, weele haue these crownes wench I warrant thee: stay, who comes here? some Irish villaine me thinkes that enter the Irish man with his master slaine. has slaine a man, and drawes him out of the way to rifle him: stand close Doll, weele see the end. The Irish man falls to rifle his master. Alas poe mester, S. Rishard Lee, be saint Patricke is rob and cut thy trote, for dee shaine, and dy money, and dee gold ring, be me truly is loue thee wel, but now dow be kil thee, bee shit ten kanaue. Sirra, sirra, you are a damned rogue, you haue kil led a man here, and rifled him of all that he has, sbloud you rogue deliuer, or ile not leaue you so much as an Irish haire a boue your shoulders, you whorson Irish dogge, sirra vntrusse presently, come off and dispatch, or by this crosse ile fetch your head off as cleane as a barke. Auant you rascal, go sirra, be walking, come Doll the diuel laughes, when one theefe robs another, come madde wench, weele to saint Albons, and reuel in our bower, hey my braue girle. Trust me, my Lord Bishop, whether Irish, Or English, Harpoole or not Harpoole, that I leaue to be decided by the triall: But sure I am this man by face and speech Is he that murdred yong sir Richard Lee: I met him presently vpon the fact, And that he slew his maister for that gold, Those iewells, and that chaine I tooke from him. I thanke your Lordship. Yes my good Lords, no sooner had he slaine His louing master for dthe wealth he had, But I vpon the instant met with him, And what he purchacde with the losse of bloud, With strokes I presently bereau'de him of, Some of the which is spent, the rest remaining, I willingly surrender to the hands Of old sir Richard Lee, as being his, Beside my Lord Iudge, I greet your honor, With letters from my Lord of Winchester. deliuers a letter. Oh but my Lord, he repents, sir Iohn repents he will mend. I thanke your good Lordship.
speeches.1: God help, God help, there's law for punishing, But theres no law for our necessity: There be more stockes to set poore soldiers in, Than there be houses to releeue them at. It is a hard world the while. We must hie vs then. I maruell that my lord should stay so long. Murther, murther murther. This ruffian seruant to sir Iohn Old-castle was like to haue slaine my Lord. And so he did.
speeches.Old man: Faith, housekeeping decayes in euery place, Euen as Saint Peter writ, still worse and worse If a poore man come to a doore to aske for Gods sake, they aske him for a licence, or a certificate from a Iustice.
speeches.4: Maister maior of Rochester has giuen commaunde ment, that none shall goe abroade out of the parish, and they haue set an order downe forsooth, what euery poore houshol der must giue towards our reliefe: where there be some ceased I may say to you, had almost as much neede to beg as we. And yet, as lame as I am, Ile with the king into France, if I can crawle but a ship-boorde, I hadde rather be slaine in France, than starue in England. God blesse him, there be but few such.
speeches.2: Faith we haue none, but what we beare vppon our bo dies, our maimed limbs, God help vs. We will attend your worship here without. He hath sent to seeke vs, I dare lay my life. Downe with him. they fight. Here he was euen now.
Ha, were I but as lusty as I was at the battell of Shrewsbury, I would not doe as I do: but we are now come to the good lord Cobhams, to the best man to the poore that is in all Kent.
Thou peeuish froward man, what wouldst thou haue? Yea, except thou haue a crue of seely knaues, And sturdy rogues, still feeding at my gate, There is no hospitalitie with thee. Tis long then of such hungry knaues as you, pointing to the beggars Yea sir, heres your retinue, your guests be come, They know their howers I warrant you. Now sir, here be your Almes knights. Now are you as safe as the Emperour. Comfort your selfe my lord, I warrant you. Peace you old foole, sirra, conuey this gentleman in the backe way, and bring the other into the walke. I thought as much, that it would not be long before I heard of something from the King, about this matter. A deed of clemencie, Your Highnesse pardon for Lord Powesse life, Which I did beg, and you my noble Lord, Of gracious fauour did vouchsafe to grant. Not yet my Liege. one ready with pen and incke. Vpon mine honor so, no otherwise. Prelate, thou liest, euen in thy greasie maw, Or whosoeuer twits me with the name, Of either traitor, or of heretike. Last night my Lord. I humbly bid farewell vnto my liege. Exit Farewell my noble lordes: my noble lords? My noble villaines, base conspirators, How can they looke his Highnesse in the face, Whome they so closly study to betray? But ile not sleepe vntill I make it knowne. This head shall not be burdned with such thoughts, Nor in this heart will I conceale a deede Of such impietie against my king. Madam, how now? Enter Harpoole and the rest. Long life and prosperous raigne vnto my Lord. Of treason mightie prince, your grace mistakes, I hope it is but in the way of mirth. Rebellion good my Lord, I know of none. Speake sirs, not one but all, I craue no fauour, Haue euer I beene conuersant with you, Or written letters to incourage you, Or kindled but the least or smallest part, Of this your late vnnaturall rebellion? Speake for I dare the vttermost you can.
This pride, this pride, brings all to beggarie, I seru'de your father, and your grandfather, Shew me such two men now: no, no, Your backes, your backes, the diuell and pride, Has cut the throate of all good housekeeping, They were the best Yeomens masters, that Euer were in England. They may sit at the gate well enough, but the diuell of any thing you giue them, except they will eate stones. My Almes knights: nay, th'are yours, It is a shame for you, and Ile stand too't, Your foolish almes maintaines more vagabonds, Then all the noblemen in Kent beside. Out you rogues, you knaues, worke for your liuings, Alas poore men, O Lord, they may beg their hearts out, Theres no more charitie amongst men, Then amongst so many mastiffe dogges, What make you here, you needy knaues? Away, away, you villaines. What should I giue them? you are growne so beg garly, you haue scarce a bitte of breade to giue at your doore: you talke of your religion so long, that you haue banished cha ritie from amongst you, a man may make a flaxe shop in your kitchin chimnies, for any fire there is stirring. Who I driue them hence? if I driue poore men from your doore, Ile be hangd, I know not what I may come to my selfe: yea, God help you poore knaues, ye see the world yfaith, well, you had a mother: well, God be with thee good Lady, thy soule's at rest: she gaue more in shirts and smocks to poore children, then you spend in your house, & yet you liue a beg gar too. Welcome good fellow, welcome, who wouldst thou speake with? Yes I am one of his men, but thou canst not speake with my lord. Ile tel thee that, when I know thy errand. Then keepe it to thy selfe, and walke like a knaue as thou camest. Then thou seruest him not, I beleeue, what lord is thy master? In good time, and what wouldst thou haue with my lord Cobham? Swounds you slaue, do you set vp your bills here, go to, take it downe againe, doest thou know what thou dost, dost thee know on whom thou seruest processe? I am glad thou knowest him yet, and sirra dost not thou know, that the lord Cobham is a braue lord, that keepes good beefe and beere in his house, and euery day feedes a hundred poore people at's gate, and keepes a hundred tall fel lowes? Mary this sir, is this processe parchment ▪ And this seale waxe? If this be parchment, & this wax, eate you this parch ment, and this waxe, or I will make parchment of your skinne, and beate your braines into waxe: Sirra Sumner dispatch, deuoure, sirra deuoure. Sirra, no railing, but betake you to your teeth, thou shalt eate no worse then thou bringst with thee, thou bringst it for my lord, and wilt thou bring my lord worse then thou wilt eate thy selfe? O do you sir me now, all's one for that, but ile make you eate it, for bringing it. Can you not? sbould ile beate you vntil you haue a stomacke. he beates him. Be champping, be chawing sir, or Ile chaw you, you rogue, the purest of the hony. O Lord sir, oh oh, he eates. Feed, feed, wholsome rogue, wholsome. Cannot you like an honest Sumner walke with the diuell your brother, to fetch in your Bailiffes rents, but you must come to a noble mans house with processe? Sbloud if thy seale were as broad as the lead that couers Rochester church, thou shouldst eate it. Who's within there? wil you shame my Lord, is there no beere in the house? Butler I say. Giue him Beere. he drinkes. There, tough old sheepskins, bare drie meate. Yea mary sir, so I meane you shall eate more then your own word, for ile make you eate all the words in the pro cesse. Why you drab monger, cannot the secrets of al the wen ches in a sheire serue your turne, but you must come hither with a citation with a poxe? Ile cite you. he has then d • ne. A cup of sacke for the Sumner. Here slaue I drinke to thee. Now if thou findst thy stomacke well, because thou shalt see my Lord keep's meate in's house, if thou wilt go in thou shalt haue a peece of beefe to thy break fast. I am glad on't, th • n be walking towards Rochester to keepe your stomack warme: and Sumner, if I may know you disturb a good wench within this Diocesse, if I do not make thee eate her peticote, if there were four yards of Kentish cloth in't, I am a villaine. Farewell Sumner. Enter Const • ble. Welcome Constable, welcom Constable, what news with thee? Hast thou bin at the Alchouse, hast thou sought there? An honest Constable, an honest Constable, cal forth him that keepes the Alchouse there. Sirra, what strangers do you lodge, there is a robbery done this morning, and we are to search for all suspected per sons. What, is he here in thy house now? Bring her forth Constable, bring her forth, let's see her, let's see her. Welcome sweete lasse, welcome. A plump girle by the mas, a plump girle, ha Dol ha, wilt thou forsake the priest, and go with me. Ye old mad mery Constable, art thou aduis'de of that ha, well said Dol, fill some ale here. Oh you o • d mad colt, yfaith Ile feak you: fil all the pots in the house there. Ha Dol, thou hast a sweete paire of lippes by the masse. Fill sweete Doll, Ile drinke to thee. imbracing her Doll, canst thou loue me? a mad mer ry lasse, would to God I had neuer seene thee. No licking for you Constable, hand off, hand off. Priest, she shal not. Vicar, Ile sit here in spight of thee, is this fitte stuffe for a priest to carry vp and downe with him? You whooreson ston'd Vicar. Swounds Vicar, Ile geld you. flies vpon him. You whooreson bawdy priest. Thou art a theefe I warrant thee. Thou art the madst priest that euer I met with. Well said mad priest, weele in and be friends, exeunt. Shall I attend your lordship to the court? Be of good cheere my Lord, if they be foes weele scramble shrewdly with them, if they be friends they are wel come: one of th • m (my Lord, Warden) is your friend, but me thinkes my ladie weepes, I like not that. Treason M. Shrieue, sbloud what treason? Patience good madame, things at worst will mend, And if they doe not, yet our liues may end. O that I had the Bishop in that feare, aside That once I had his Sumner by our selues. Sbloud my lord Bishop, ye do me wrong, I am nei ther heretike nor puritane, but of the old church, ile sweare, drinke ale, kisse a wench, go to masse, eate fish all Lent, and fast fridaies with cakes and wine, fruite and spicerie, shriue me of my old sinnes afore Easter, and beginne new afore whitson tide. That knaue was simply put vpon the Bishop. But doe not Sumner as voule answere it, for I haue there English bookes my lord, that ile not part with for your Bishoppricke, Beuis of Hampton, Owleglasse, the Frier and the Boy, Ellen of Rumming, Robin hood, and other such godly stories which if ye burne, by this flesh ile make ye drink their ashes in S. Margets ale. exeunt. Who calls there? I will sir. Nothing but to borrow your vpper garments a lit tle; not a word more, for if you do, you die: peace, for waking the children, there, put them on, dispatch, my lord, the window that goes out into the leads, is sure enough, I told you that be fore, there, make you ready, ile conuay him after, and bind him surely in the inner roome. Heere my Lord, come come away. I beseech you good my lord of Rochester, be fauo rable to my lord and maister. Heare me my Lord, hard vnder Islington wait you my comming, I will bring my Lady ready, with horses to conuay you hence. Nay my good lord of Rochester, ile bring you to S. Albons through the woods, I warrant you. Nay since I am past the Towers libertie, thou part'st not so. be drawes. You cowardly rogues. sir Iohn escapes. Stand off if you loue your puddings. There, now it workes, then let me speed, for now is the fittest time for me to scape away. exit Well mine hoste, I pray thee helpe mee to a payre of faire sheetes, and Ile go lodge with him. VVho calles there? Yes mary doe I, zwounds, I can not finde my hose, this Irish rascall that was lodgde with me all night, hath stolne my apparell, and has left me nothing but a lowsie mantle, and a paire of broags. Get vp, get vp, and if the carier and his wench be asleep, change you with them as he hath done with me, and see if we can escape. What art thou that bidst me stand? Sbloud Constable, art thou madde? am I an Irish man? I faith my Lord, I am in, get out how I can. Yea, yea my lord, Harpoole is so resolude, I wreake of death the lesse, in that I die Not by the sentence of that enuious priest The Bishop of Rochester, oh were it he, Or by his meanes that I should suffer here, It would be double torment to my soule.
God blesse your honour, God saue the good Lord Cobham, and all his house, Iesu defend me, Is't possible your cunning could so temper The princely disposition of his mind, To signe the damage of a royall subiect? Well, the best is, it beares an ancedate, Procured by my absence, and your malice, But I, since that, haue shewd my selfe as true, As any churchman that dare challenge me, Let me be brought before his maiestie, If he acquite me not, then do your worst. What meane you sir to trouble weary soules, And interrupt vs of our quiet sleepe? Oh giue me patience to indure this scourge, Thou that art fountaine of that vertuous streame, And though contempt, false witnes, and reproch Hang on these yron gyues, to presse my life As low as earth, yet strengthen me with faith, That I may mount in spirite aboue the cloudes. Here comes my lady, sorow tis for her, Thy wound is greeuous, else I scoffe at thee. What and poore Harpoole! art thou ith bryars too? What will that helpe vs? being knowne, sweete loue, VVe shall for heresie be put to death, For so they tearme the religion we professe. No, if it be ordained we must die, And at this instant, this our comfort be, That of the guilt imposde, our soules are free. No Cobha ̄ now, nor madam as you loue vs, But Iohn of Lancashire, and Ione his wife. That we are free from murders very thought, And know not how the gentleman was slaine. Iournying my lord from London from the terme, Downe into Lancashire where we do dwell, And what with age and trauell being faint, VVe gladly sought a place where we might rest, Free from resort of other passengers, And so we strayed into that secret corner. Tis true my Lord, and God forgiue him for it.
Good your honour, bestow your blessed almes, Vpon poore men.
I beseech you sit, be good to vs.
speeches.Cobham: Nay, nay, they know thee well enough, I thinke that all the beggars in this land are thy acquaintance, goe bestowe your almes, none will controule you sir. If thou wilt giue them nothing, send them hence, let them not stand here staruing in the colde. Euen the worst deede that ere my mother did, was in releeuing such a foole as thou. Go you olde foole, giue the poore people some thing, go in poore men into the inner court, and take such alms as there is to be had. What fellow's yonder comes along the groue? Few passengers there be that know this way: Me thinkes he stops as though he stayd for me, And meant to shrowd himselfe amongst the bushes. I know the Cleargie hate me to the death, And my religion gets me many foes: And this may be some desperate rogue, Subornd to worke me mischiefe: As it Pleaseth God, if he come toward me, sure Ile stay his comming, be he but one man, What soere he be: The Lord Powis comes on. I haue beene well acquainted with that face. You are welcome sir, what ere you be, But of this sodaine sir, I do not know you. My honorable lord, and worthy friend, What makes your lordship thus alone in Kent, And thus disguised in this strange attire? I hope no man was violently slaine. I am sory, my good lord, of these ill newes. Your lordship is most welcome vnto Cobham, But I am very sory, my good lord, My name was brought in question in this matter, Considering I haue many enemies, That threaten malice, and do lie in waite To take aduantange of the smallest thing. But you are welcome, and repose your lordship, And keepe your selfe here secret in my house, Vntill we heare how the lord Herbert speedes: Here comes my man. Enter Harpoole. Sirra, what newes? My gracious Lord vnto your Maiestie, Next vnto my God, I owe my life, And what is mine, either by natures gift, Or fortunes bountie, al is at your seruice, But for obedience to the Pope of Rome, I owe him none, nor shall his shaueling priests That are in England, alter my beliefe. If out of holy Scripture they can proue, That I am in an errour, I will yeeld, And gladly take instruction at their hands, But otherwise, I do beseech your grace, My conscience may not be incroacht vpon. My liege, if any breathe, that dares come forth, And say, my life in any of these points Deserues th'attaindor of ignoble thoughts Here stand I, crauing no remorce at all, But euen the vtmost rigor may be showne. All night or day it must be so, sweete wife, Vrge me not why or what my businesse is, But get you in: Lord Powesse, beare with me, And madam, thinke your welcome nere the worse: My house is at your vse. Harpoo • e, away. What will these Ostlers sleepe all day? Good morow, good morow, Come wench, come, Saddle, saddle, now afore God too foord-dayes, ha? What, will no body open the gates here? Come, lets int stable to looke to our capons.
speeches.Harpoole: Yea, yea, I am a foole still, with all your wit you will die a beggar, go too. Hang you roags, hang you, theres nothing but misery amongst you, you feare no law you. Exit. Yonders one maister Butler of the priuie cham ber, is sent vnto you from the King. Fellow, what ailes thee? doost thou quake? dost thou shake? dost thou tremble? ha? Come sir. you are welcome, if you loue my lorde. Sir, yonder my lord walkes, you see him, Ile haue your men into the Celler the while. What, hast thou neuer an empty roome in thy house for me?
speeches.Olde man: God blesse you good maister Rafe, God saue your life, you are good to the poore still.
speeches.Powis: Well met my honorable lord and friend. I am one that wisheth well vnto your honor, My name is Powes, an olde friend of yours. My Lord, an vnexpected accident, Hath at this time inforc'de me to these parts: And thus it hapt, not yet ful fiue dayes since, Now at the last Assise at Hereford, It chanst that the lord Herbert and my selfe, Mongst other things, discoursing at the table, To fall in speech about some certaine points Of Wickcliffes doctrine, gainst the papacie, And the religion catholique, maintaind Through the most part of Europe at this day. This wilfull teasty lord stucke not to say, That Wickcliffe was a knaue, a schismatike, His doctrine diuelish and hereticall, And what soere he was maintaind the same, was traitor both to God and to his country. Being moued at his peremptory speech, I told him, some maintained those opinions, Men, and truer subiects then lord Herbert was: And he replying in comparisons: Your name was vrgde, my lord, gainst his chalenge, To be a perfect fauourer of the trueth. And to be short, from words we fell to blowes, Our seruants, and our tenants taking parts, Many on both sides hurt: and for an houre The broyle by no meanes could be pacified, Vntill the Iudges rising from the bench, Were in their persons forc'de to part the fray. Faith none I trust, but the lord Herberts selfe, Who is in truth so dangerously hurt, As it is doubted he can hardly scape. This is the cause that driues me into Kent, To shrowd my selfe with you so good a friend, Vntill I heare how things do speed at home. I pray God the lord Herbert be not dead, and the King hearing whither I am gone, hath sent for me. God haue mercy gentle friend. exeunt.
welcome good maister Butler. God blesse his Highnesse, and confound his enne mies, I hope his Maiestie is well. God long continue it: mee thinkes you looke as though you were not well, what ailes you sir? I am very sorie sir for your mischance, wee will send our warrant foorth, to stay such suspitious persons as shal be found, then maister Butler, we wil attend you. My lord of Cambridge? Your honor is most welcome into Kent, And all the rest of this faire company. I am new come from London, gentle • ordes: But will ye not take Cowling for your host, And see what entertainement it affordes? Businesse my lord? what businesse should you haue But to be mery? we haue no delicates, But this Ile promise you, a peece of venison, A cup of wine, and so forth: hunters fare: And if you please, weele strike the stagge our selues Shall fill our dishes with his wel-fed flesh. My lordes, and you shall haue your choice with me. Tis pitty such a goodly beast should die. Faith Lords, I like the pastime, wheres the place? Call ye this hunting, my lords? Is this the stag You faine would chase, Harry our dread king? So we may make a banquet for the diuell, And in the fleede of wholsome meate, prepare A dish of poison to confound our selues. Notorious treason! yet I will conceale aside My secret thought • , to sound the depth of it. My lord of Cambridge, I doe see your claime, And what good may redound vnto the land, By prosecuting of this enterprise. • ut where are men? where's power and furniture To order such an action? we are weake, Harry, you know's a mighty potentate. Some likelihoode, I must confesse, to speede: • ut how shall I beleeue this is plaine truth? You are (my lords) such men as liue in Court, And highly haue beene fauour'd of the king, Especially lord Scroope, whome oftentimes He m • keth choice of for his bedfellow. And you lord Gray are of his priuy councell: Is not this a traine to intrappe my life? Nay you are noble men, and I imagine, As you a • e honorable by birth and bloud, So you will be in heart, in thought, in word. I craue no other testimony but this. That you wou • d all subscribe, and set your hands Vnto this writing which you gaue to me. Sir, let me craue, That you would likewise write your name with theirs, For confirmation of your maisters word, The king of Fraunce. So now this action is well knit together, And I am for you: where`s our meeting, lords? In Kent? agreed: now let vs in to supper, I hope your honors will not away to night. Yet taste a cup of wine before ye go. Madam, not so: there is your husbands pardon, Long may ye liue, each ioy vnto the other. • et that alone: and madam stay me not, For I must backe vnto the court againe With all the speede I can: Harpoole, my horse. Yea sir, your gelding, mount you presently exe. Let this my Lord, which I present your grace Speake for my loyalty, reade these articles, And then giue sentence of my life or death. There is the platforme, and their hands, my lord, Each seuerally subscribed to the same. Harpoole, Harpoole, I heare a maruelous noyse a bout the house, God warant vs, I feare wee are pursued: what Harpoole. Tis I, dost thou not heare a noyse about the house?
speeches.Butler: Thankes, my good lord: his Maiestie dooth com mend his loue vnto your lordship, and wils you to repaire vn to the court. In health, my lord. Faith I haue had a foolish odde mischance, that an gers mee: comming ouer Shooters hill, there came a fellow to me like a Sailer, and asked me money, and whilst I staide my horse to draw my purse, he takes th'aduantage of a little banck and leapes behind me, whippes my purse away, and with a so daine ierke I know not how, threw me at least three yards out of my saddle. I neuer was so robbed in all my life. I humbly thanke your lordship, I will attend you.
I haue the law to warrant what I do, and though the Lord Cobham be a noble man, that dispenses not with law, I dare serue processe were a fiue noble men, though we Sum ners make sometimes a mad slip in a corner with a prettie wench, a Sumner must not goe alwayes by seeing, a manne may be content to hide his eies, where he may feele his profit: well, this is my Lord Cobhams house, if I can deuise to speake with him, if not, Ile clap my citation vpon's doore, so my lord of Rochester bid me, but me thinkes here comes one of his men. Enter Harpoole. With my lord Cobham, I would speake, if thou be one of his men. May I send to him them? I will not tel my errand to thee. I tell thee my lord keepes no knaues, sirra. My lord of Rochester. I come by vertue of a processe, to ascite him to ap peare before my lord, in the court at Rochester. Why, if he will not be spoken withall, then will I leaue it here, and see you that he take knowledge of it. Yes marry doe I, Sir Iohn Old-castle Lord Cob ham. Whats that to my processe? Yes mary. It is so. I am my lord of Rochesters Sumner, I came to do my office, and thou shalt answere it. Sir, I brought it not my lord to eate. I cannot eate it. O hold, hold, good master seruing-man, I will eate it. Tough waxe, is the purest of the hony. O I am almost choaked, I am almost choaked. O sir, let me go no further, Ile eate my word. I thanke you sir. No I am very well good M. seruing-man, I thanke you, very well sir. God be with you M. seruingmaan.
speeches.Harp: Wel, God grant me patience, I could eate this conger. My lord is not at home, therefore it were good Sum ner you caried your processe backe. O that it were the blessed will of God, that thou and I were within twenty mile of it, on Salisbury plaine! I would lose my head if euer thou broughtst thy head hither a gaine. aside. His case is hard my lord, you shall safely get out of the Tower, but I will downe vpon them, in which time get you away.
God saue you M. Harpoole. And't please you M. Harpoole, I am to make hue to crie, for a fellow with one eie that has rob'd two Clothiers, and am to craue your hindrance, for to search all suspected places, and they say there was a woman in the company. I durst not search sir, in my Lord Cobhams libertie, except I had some of his seruants, which are for my warrant. Ho, who's within there? She is sir, I promise you sir he is a quiet man, and be cause he will not trouble too many roomes, he makes the wo man lie euery night at his beds feete. Dorothy, you must come downe to M. Constable. A well said M. Harpoole, you are a merrie old man yfaith, yfaith you wil neuer be old: now by the macke, a prettie wench indeed. Oh wel said M. Harpoole, you are heart of oake when all's done. Come you villainous heretique, confesse where you • maister is. VVheres the lord Cobham sir Iohn Old-castle tha • lately is escaped out of the Tower. Ahone, you crafty rascall? exeunt. Stand close, heere comes the Irish man that didde the murther, by all tokens, this is he. I am the Officer, and am come to search for an Irish man, such a villaine as thy selfe, that hast murthered a man this last night by the hie way. Make him fast: O thou bloudy rogue! Who comes there? VVho comes heere?
speeches.Ale man: Who calls there, come neere a Gods name, oh is't you M. Constable and M. Harpoole, you are welcome with all my heart, what make you here so earely this morning? Holde, as you are men, holde, for Gods sake be quiet: put vp your weapons, you drawe not in my house.
Gods bores, I am sory for't, yfaith sir I lodge no bo dy but a good honest mery priest, they call him sir Iohn a Wrootham, and a handsome woman that is his neece, that he saies he has some sute in law for, and as they go vp & down to London, sometimes they lie at my house.
A non forsooth. she enters. I thank you good M. seruing-man, and master Con stable also.
speeches.Dol: Oh if I wist this old priest would not sticke to me, by Ioue I would ingle this old seruing-man.
speeches.Doll: Truely you are a most sweet olde man, as euer I sawe, by my troth, you haue a face, able to make any woman in loue with you. I pledge you sir, and thanke you therefore, and I pray you let it come. I warrant you you will not out of my thoughts this tweluemonth, truely you are as full of fauour, as a man may be. Ah these sweete grey lockes, by my troth, they are most louely. Oh you are an od boie, you haue a wanton eie of your owne: ah you sweet sugar lipt wanton, you will winne as ma ny womens hearts as come in your company. Enter Priest. Ile come anone, sweete loue. Murder, murder, murder. Come, be quiet, hast thou sped? Come, lets be all friends then. I am as true to thee, as the stone is in the wal, and thou knowest well enough sir Iohn, I was in as good doing, when I came to thee, as any wench neede to be: and therefore thou hast tried me, that thou hast: by Gods body, I wil not be kept as I haue bin, that I will not. What is al the gold spent you tooke the last day from the Courtier? You might haue left me at Cobham, vntil you had bin better prouided for. Ah thou art a mad priest yfaith. Why is all the gold spent already that you had the o ther day? You might haue left me in Kent, that you might, vntil you had bin better prouided, I could haue sta • ed at Cobham. Faith sir Iohn, I might haue gone to seruice againe, old maister Harpoole told me he would prouide me a mistris. O thou art old sir Iohn, when all's done yfaith.
speeches.Constable: Gods boores maister Harpoole, I will haue one busse too. Bur lady I loue kissing as wel as you. Keepe the Kings peace. Hold sir Iohn, hold. Well said mistris Dorothy ifaith.
Doll, come hither. Hand off, old fornicator. You olde stale ruffin, you lion of Cotswold. You old mutton monger. Then I am but as thou hast beene in thy dayes, lets not be ashamed of our trade, the King has beene a theefe him selfe. I haue wench, here be crownes ifaith. Giue me thy hand, thou art as good a fellow, I am a singer, a drinker, a bencher, a wencher, I can say a masse, and kisse a lasse: faith I haue a parsonage, and bicause I would not be at too much charges, this wench serues me for a sexton.
speeches.Wrotham: Ah sirra, dost thou not know, that a good fellow parson may haue a chappel of ease, where his parish Church is farre off?
speeches.Doll to the Priest: I pray thee sweet heart be quiet, I was but sitting to drinke a pot of ale with him, euen as kinde a man as euer I met with.
speeches.Acton: Now maister Murley, I am well assurde You know our arrant, and do like the cause, Being a man affected as we are? You know our faction now is growne so great, Throughout the realme; that it beginnes to smoake Into the Cleargies eies, and the Kings eares, High time it is that we were drawne to head, Our generall and officers appoynted. And warres ye wot will aske great store of coine. Able to strength our action with your purse, You are elected for a colonell Ouer a regiment of fifteene bands. Why who but he shall be our Generall? My word for that, sir William Murley knight. There are of vs, our friends, and followers, Three thousand and three hundred at the least, Of northerne lads foure thousand, beside horse, From Kent there comes with sir Iohn Old-castle Seauen thousand, then from London issue out, Of maisters, seruants, strangers, prentices Fortie odde thousands into Ficket field, Where we appoynt our speciall randeuous. Behinde saint Giles in the field neere Holbo • ne. On friday next the foureteenth day of Ianuary. Fiue hundreth man? fiue thousand's not enough, A hundreth thousand will not pay our men Two months together, either come preparde Like a braue Knight, and martiall Colonell, In glittering golde, and gallant furniture, Bringing in coyne, a cart loade at the least, And all your followers mounted on good horse, Or neuer come disgracefull to vs all. See what Ambition may perswade men to, In hope of honor he will spend himselfe. Thats no fault in Brewers now-adayes: Come, away about our businesse. exeunt. Now tis too late to haue it remedied, I prithee Murley doe not vrge me with it.
Mary God dild ye daintie my deere, no master, good • r Roger Acton Knight, maister Bourne, and maister Beuer ley esquires, gentlemen, and iustices of the peace, no maister I, but plaine William Murly the brewer of Dunstable your ho nest neighbour, and your friend, if ye be men of my professi on.
speeches.Beuerley: Professed friends to Wickliffe, foes to Rome. Nay maister Murley, if you obserue such daies, We make some question of your constancie, All daies are like to men resolu'de in right. Perchance you may be chosen Treasurer, Tenne thousand pounds the least that you can bring. Was neuer bankerout Brewer yet but one, With vsing too much mault, too little water.
Hold by me lad, leane vpon that staffe good mai ster Beuerley, all of a house, say your mind, say your mind. Friends and fellowes indeede sir Roger. Be it more or lesse, what a world is this? Would I had continued still of the order of knaues, And neuer sought knighthood, since it costes So deere: sir Roger, I may thanke you for all. Fy paltry paltry, to and fro, as occasion serues, If you be so hasty take my place. I could be glad to giue my betters place. Exeunt.
speeches.Murley: Fue paltrie paltrie, in and out, to and fro, be it more or lesse, vppon occasion, Lorde haue mercie vppon vs, what a world is this? Sir Roger Acton, I am but a Dunstable man, a plaine brewer, ye know: will lusty Caualiering captaines gen tlemen come at my calling, goe at my bidding? Daintie my deere, theile doe a dogge of waxe, a horse of cheese, a pricke and a pudding, no, no, ye must appoint some lord or knight at least to that place. Mary God dild ye daintie my deare: But tell me, who shalbe our Generall? Wheres the lord Cobham, sir Iohn Old-castle, That noble almes-giuer, housekeeper, vertuous, Religious gentleman? Come to me there boies, Come to me there. And shall he knight me, and make me colonell? Fellow sir Roger Acton knight, all fellowes, I meane in armes, how strong are we? how many partners? our e • emies beside the King are mightie, be it more or lesse vpon occasion, reckon our force. Newgate, vp Holborne, S. Giles in the field, and to Tiborne, an old saw: for the day, for the day? Tyllie vallie, trust me neuer if I haue any liking of that day: fue paltry paltry, friday quoth a, dismall day, Chil dermasse day this yeare was friday. Say Amen, and say no more, but say, and hold ma ster Beuerley, friday next, and Ficket field, and William Mur ley, and his merry men shalbe al one, I haue halfe a score iades that draw my beere cartes, and euery iade shall beare a knaue, and euery knaue shall weare a iacke, and euery iacke shal haue a scull, and euery scull shal shew a speare, and euery speare shal kill a foe at Ficket field, at Ficket field, Iohn and Tom, and Dicke and Hodge, and Rafe and Robin, William & George, and all my knaues shall fight like men, at Ficket field on friday next. It may be modestly, decently, soberly, and hand somely I may bring fiue hundreth pound. Paltry paltry, in and 〈◊〉 and fro, 〈…〉 I haue ten thousand pound to 〈◊〉 , and 〈…〉 ra ther than the Bishop shall haue 〈◊〉 will of mee for my consci ence, it shall out all. Flame and flaxe, flame and flaxe, it was gotte with water and mault, and it shal flie with fire and gunne powder. Sir Roger, a cart loade of mony til the axetree cracke, my selfe and my men in Ficket field on friday next: remem ber my Knighthoode, and my place: there's my hand Ile bee there. Exit.
speeches.Bourne: Why master Murley, you shall be a Knight: Were you not in election to be shrieue? Haue ye not past all offices but that? Haue ye not wealth to make your wife a lady? I warrant you, my lord, our Generall Bestowes that honor on you at first sight. What summe of money meane you to disburse? I neuer thought a Brewer halfe so • ich. Yet our action stands, Sir Roger Acton may supply his place.
speeches.〈◊〉: 〈…〉 paltry, in and out to and fro, Lord haue 〈…〉 a world is this, wheres that Ficket fielde, sir Roger?
Sir Roger Acton, and a crue, my Lord, Of bold seditious rebels, are in Armes, Intending reformation of Religion. And with their Army they intend to pitch, In Ficket field, vnlesse they be repulst. Their number is not knowne, as yet (my Lord) But tis reported Sir Iohn Old-castle Is the chiefe man, on whom they do depend. Yes my gracious Lord. It is my Lord, Your noble Vncle Exceter is there, Your brother Gloucester and my Lord of Warwicke, Who with the maior and the Aldermen, Do guard the gates, and keepe good rule within, The Earle of Cambridge, and sir Thomas Gray, Do walke the Round, Lord Scroope and Butler skout, So though it please your maiestie to iest, Were you in bed, well might you take your rest, I must haue the dice, What do we play at? the play at dice. Set round then, so, at all. Harry you passe indeede for you sweepe all. It may be so, but we beleeue it not. Set round, at all. What, halfe a broken angell? That when he robs againe, he shall be hang'd. Will you away, and make no more to do? No good sir knight, you shall begin in your hand.
Once more my Lord of Cambridge make rehersal, How you do stand intiteled to the Crowne, The deeper shall we print it in our mindes, And euery man the better be resolu'de, When he perceiues his quarrell to be iust.
Then thus Lord Scroope, sir Thomas Gray, & you Mounsieur de Cha • tres, agent for the French, This Lionell Duke of Clarence, as I said, Third sonne of Edward (Englands King) the third H • d issue Phillip his sole daughter and heyre, Which Phillip afterward was giuen in marriage, To Edmund Mortimer the Earle of March, And by him had a son cald Roger Mortimer, Which Roger likewise had of his discent, Edmund, Roger, Anne, and Elianor, Two daughters and two sonnes, but those three Dide without issue, Anne that did suruiue, And now was left her fathers onely heyre, My fortune was to marry, being too By my grandfather of King Edwardes line, So of his sirname, I am calde you know, Richard Plantagenet, my father was, Edward the Duke of Yorke, and son and heyre To Edmund Langley, Edward the third's first sonne. True, for this Harry, and his father both Harry the first, as plainely doth appeare, Are false intruders, and vsurp the Crowne. For when yong Richard was at Pomfret slaine, In him the title of prince Edward dide, That was the eldest of king Edwards sonnes: William of Hatfield, and their second brother, Death in his nonage had before bereft: So that my wife deriu'd from Lionell, Third sonne vnto king Edward, ought proceede, And take possession of the Diademe Before this Harry, or his father king, Who fetcht their title but from Lancaster, Forth of that royall line. And being thus, What reason ist but she should haue her right?
speeches.Scroop: So that it seemes your claime comes by your wife, As lawfull heyre to Roger Mortimer, The son of Edmund, which did marry Phillip Daughter and heyre to Lyonell Duke of Clarence. What thinke ye then of this? I am his bedfellow, And vnsuspected nightly sleepe with him. VVhat if I venture in those silent houres, VVhen sleepe hath sealed vp all mortall eies, To murder him in bed? how like ye that? What shal we rise thus, and determine nothing?
speeches.Scroope: I am resolu'de our enterprise is iust. No more earle Cambridge, here I plight my faith, To set vp thee, and thy renowned wife. A ready way: here comes the man himselfe Booted and spurrd, it seemes he hath beene riding. That is indeede the thing we all desire. How say you then, will you first hunt with vs? • esides, you know your selfe is in disgrace, Held as a recreant, and pursude to death. This will defend you from your enemies, And stablish your religion through the land. VVeele sweare to you. My pocket should haue one: yea, heere it is. And there is my name. And we would not be absent from the court, Lest thereby grow suspition in the king.
speeches.Gray: Harry shall die, or else resigne his crowne. That haue I my Lord. Or take the sacrament. And mine. But yet there may be doubt in their deliuery, Harry is wise, therefore Earle of Cambridge, I Iudge that way not so conuenient. VVhy any of these, or if you will, Ile cause a present sitting of the Councell, VVherein I will pretend some matter of such weight, As needes must haue his royall company, And to dispatch him in the Councell chamber.
Performe but that, and Charles the king of France Shall ayde you lordes, not onely with his men, But send you money to maintaine your warres, Fiue hundred thousand crownes he bade me proffer, If you can stop but Harries voyage for France. And to assist ye, as I said before, Charters doth gage the honor of his king.
speeches.Scrope: We neuer had a fitter time than now The realme in such diuision as it is.
Besides, you must perswade ye there is due, Vengeance for Richards murder, which although It be defende, yet will it fall at last, And now as likely as another time. Sinne hath had many yeeres to ripen in, And now the haruest cannot be farre off, Wherein the weedes of vsurpation, Are to be cropt, and cast into the fire. Doubt not of him, my lord, his life's pursu'de By th'incensed Cleargy, and of late, • rought in displeasure with the king, assures He may be quickly wonne vnto our faction. Who hath the articles were drawne at large Of our whole purpose? We should not now be farre off from his house, Our serious conference hath beguild the way, See where his castle stands, giue me the writing. When we are come vnto the speech of him, Because we will not stand to make recount, Of that which hath beene saide, here he shall reade enter Co • . Our mindes at large, and what we craue of him. VVell met lord Cobham. We were intended to haue beene your guests: But now this lucky mee • ing shall suffise To end our businesse, and deferre that kindnesse. Nay but the stagge which we desire to strike, Liues not in Cowling: if you will consent, And goe with vs, weele bring you to a forrest, Where runnes a lusty hierd: amongst the which There is a stagge superior to the rest, A stately beast, that when his fellows runne, He leades the race, and beates the sullen earth, As though he sco • nd it with his trampling hoofes, Aloft he beares his head, and with his breast, Like a huge bulwarke counter-checkes the wind: And when he standeth still, he stretcheth forth His prowd ambitious necke, as if he meant To wound the firmament with forked hornes. Not so, sir Iohn, for he is tyrannous, And gores the other deere, and will not keep Within the limites are appointed him. Of late hees broke into a seueral, Which doth belong to me, and there he spoiles Both corne and pasture, two of his wilde race Alike sor stealth, and couetous incroatching, Already are remou'd, if he were dead, I should not onely be secure from hurt, But with his body make a royall feast. Peruse this writing, it will shew you all, And what occasion we haue for the sport. he reades Why so lord Cobham? see you not our claime? And how imperiously he holdes the crowne? Tut, we are strong enough, you are belou'de, And many will be glad to follow you, VVe are the light, and some will follow vs: Besides, there is hope from France: heres an embassador That promiseth both men and money too. The commons likewise (as we heare) pretend A sodaine tumult, we wil ioyne with them. Then perish may my soule: wh • t thinke you so? VVith all our hearts: who hath any pen and inke? Giue it me lord Scroope: there is my name. Here if you please, the tenth of Iuly next. Yes present • y, for I haue farre to ride, About solliciting of other friends. Not now my lord, we thanke you: so farewell. In mine opinion, Scroope hath well aduisde, Poison will be the only aptest meane, And fittest for our purpose to dispatch him. Herein consistes no safetie for your selfe, And you disclosde, what shall become of vs? But this day (as ye know) he will aboord, The wind so faire, and set away for France, If as he goes, or entring in the ship, It might be done, then it were excellent, Tush, yet I heare not any thing to purpose, I wonder that lord Cobham staies so long, His counsell in this case would much auaile vs.
speeches.G • i •: Gray will performe the same, as he is knight.
speeches.S • roope: We lacke but now Lord Cobhams fellowship, And then our plot were absolute indeede.
You are welcome home, my Lord, Why seeme ye so disquiet in your lookes? What hath befalne you that disquiets your minde?
Bad newes I am afraide touching my husband.
speeches.Powesse: So great a ki • dnesse as I knowe not howe to make reply, my sense is quite confounded. Though great occasion be we should departe, yet madam will we stay to be resolude, of this vnlookt for doubtful accident. Exeunt.
So soone my Lord? what will you ride all night? My husband hot with trauelling my lord, His nose gusht out a bleeding, that was it. To cut such simple victuall as we had.
I prythee Harpoole, looke vnto thy Lord, I do not like this sodaine posting backe.
speeches.Powe •: Some earnest businesse is a foote belike, What e're it be, pray God be his good guide.
Amen that hath so highly vs bested. I will withdraw into some other roome, So that your Lordship, and the rest be pleasde. I thinke no lesse, are they suspected trow ye For doing of this murder? My Lord Cobham, madam? as she passeth ouer the stage by the ̄ . Oh tel, what is it that our loue can do, To pleasure you, for we are bound to you.
